Husbandry

Health Tasks

Vaccinations, worming, foot care and common health issues.

Shepherd's YearLambingHealth TasksTupping

Vaccinations

The most important routine vaccination for Portland sheep is against clostridial diseases. A combined vaccine such as Heptavac-P Plus also covers pasteurellosis.

  • Ewes: Vaccinate 4–6 weeks before lambing. If ewes have not been vaccinated before, give a primary course of two injections 4–6 weeks apart.
  • Lambs: Lambs from vaccinated ewes receive passive immunity via colostrum. Primary vaccination at 8–10 weeks; booster 4–6 weeks later; annual boosters thereafter.

Worm Control (SCOPS principles)

Portland sheep are no more or less susceptible to internal parasites than other breeds, but as a conservation breed it is important to use anthelmintics responsibly to minimise resistance.

  • Use Faecal Egg Counts (FECs) to target treatment rather than blanket dosing
  • Avoid treating animals unnecessarily — young lambs on pasture in summer are most at risk
  • Use different anthelmintic groups in rotation and always treat to the correct weight
  • Quarantine and treat any incoming animals before mixing with the flock

Follow the SCOPS guidelines for sustainable worm control.

Foot Care

Portland sheep kept on well-drained upland or chalk pastures often require minimal foot trimming. Those on wetter lowland ground may need more regular attention.

  • Check feet at least twice yearly — at housing/pregnancy scanning and at tupping
  • Treat footrot promptly: pare affected tissue, treat with antibiotic spray, isolate affected animals
  • Vaccination against footrot (Footvax) is recommended in flocks with persistent problems
  • Avoid over-trimming — leave the white line intact

Flystrike

Blowfly strike is a serious welfare concern, particularly in warm wet weather (May–September). Portland sheep's dense fleece can harbour the conditions flystrike needs.

  • Check sheep daily in the risk season — watch for wool pulling, stamping or dark damp patches
  • Use preventive products (e.g. Crovect, CLiK) in high-risk periods
  • Dagg (crutch) ewes before the risk season to remove soiled wool around the back end
  • Treat affected sheep immediately — remove maggots, clean the wound, apply wound dressing

Common Health Issues

ConditionSignsAction
Hypocalcaemia (milk fever)Staggers, collapse in late pregnancy/early lactationIV/SC calcium borogluconate urgently
Pregnancy toxaemia (twin lamb disease)Dull, off food, wobbly gait in late pregnancyPropylene glycol, vet attention
OrfCrusty lesions around mouth/nose — also infects humansIsolate; vaccine available; wear gloves
PneumoniaCough, nasal discharge, rapid breathingVet — antibiotics required

Always consult your vet for diagnosis and treatment of sick animals. This guidance is general only and does not replace professional veterinary advice.
